intro: A stadium is a workplace for the athletes on the field. It is also a public place where thousands of citizens gather, often under a flag and a song. This unit looks at what happens when those two roles collide. You will study athletes who raised a flag, a fist or a knee, and athletes who refused to play at all, from Athens in 1906 to the NBA bubble in 2020.

The second chapter follows money. Women's and men's professional sports mostly grew as separate industries, with separate tours, leagues and sponsors. You will trace women's golf, baseball, tennis, basketball and soccer, and the fights over prize money, contracts and television time. Illinois appears through Comiskey Park, the Rockford Peaches and the Chicago Sky.

By the end you will be able to name the body that set each rule, from the IOC to the NBA to the All England Club. You will explain the difference between a gesture and a walkout, and between a parallel institution and a shared one. You will also use dates, laws, court cases and prize lists to argue a position.
bigQuestion: When athletes use the field to argue for rights or pay, whose rules decide what they may do, and how have those rules changed?

timeline.t: Wimbledon adds a ladies' singles event, seven years after its first men's championship
Peter O'Connor waves an Irish flag from a flagpole at the Athens Games
The Star-Spangled Banner is played at the World Series at Comiskey Park
Philip K. Wrigley founds a women's baseball league that includes the Rockford Peaches
Thirteen women found the Ladies Professional Golf Association
Muhammad Ali refuses induction; the Olympic Project for Human Rights forms
Smith and Carlos raise fists on the podium in Mexico City
The Original 9 sign one-dollar contracts and play in Houston
The WTA is founded, and the U.S. Open pays equal prize money
Wimbledon and the French Open adopt equal prize money
Colin Kaepernick begins kneeling during the anthem
U.S. Soccer signs equal pay agreements with its two national teams

words.d: refusing to take part in something to press for change
a protest in which workers leave their jobs together
a song a country officially adopts to stand for the nation
the IOC's founding rule book for the Olympic Movement and the Games
a person who refuses military service because of religious or moral beliefs
a formal complaint a worker files under a labor agreement
the power to influence a decision because others need something you control
tennis since 1968, when professionals were allowed into the major tournaments
a separate organization that runs alongside another, doing similar work for a different group
official approval of an event by a governing body
an organization of athletes that bargains for them as a group
a contract negotiated between employers and a union for a group of workers

test.q: What did Peter O'Connor protest at the 1906 Athens Games?
choices: Being entered as British rather than Irish
The length of the long jump runway
test.why: O'Connor waved an Irish flag because he had been entered under Great Britain.

test.q: When did the Star-Spangled Banner become the official U.S. national anthem?
test.why: President Hoover signed the law on March 3, 1931.

test.q: Who founded the Olympic Project for Human Rights with Black athletes in 1967?
test.why: Harry Edwards, a San Jose State sociology teacher, helped found the OPHR.

test.q: Why did Muhammad Ali lose his boxing license in 1967?
choices: He refused induction into the Army
test.why: Commissions suspended him after he refused induction on April 28, 1967.

test.q: Which rule book bans political demonstrations at Olympic sites?
test.why: Rule 50 of the Olympic Charter bans demonstrations and propaganda at Olympic sites.

choices: The Milwaukee Bucks did not come out for a playoff game
test.why: The Bucks stayed in the locker room after the Jacob Blake shooting, and the NBA postponed games.

test.q: How did the 1965 AFL walkout differ from the 1968 podium protest?
choices: Players refused to play instead of making a gesture during a ceremony
It was punished by the IOC
test.why: Twenty-one players left New Orleans, and the league moved the game to Houston.

test.q: Which statement is true of the Rockford Peaches?
choices: They played every season of the AAGPBL
test.why: The Illinois team played from 1943 to 1954 and won four titles.

test.q: What did the Original 9 do in 1970?
choices: Signed one-dollar contracts to play an event the national body would not sanction
test.why: They signed with Gladys Heldman and played the Houston Virginia Slims event.

test.q: Which was the first major to pay men and women equal prize money?
test.why: The U.S. Open paid both champions 25,000 dollars in 1973.

test.q: Why was the Battle of the Sexes important if it counted for no title?
choices: It changed the rules of scoring
It drew a huge crowd and national TV audience to a woman's win
test.why: More than 30,000 attended and ABC broadcast it in prime time.

test.q: What is a parallel institution in sport?
choices: A rule copied from another sport
A separate body running alongside another, such as the LPGA beside men's golf
test.why: The LPGA and WTA run women's tours alongside men's bodies.

choices: Venus Williams wins Wimbledon with equal pay
test.why: Williams won in 2007; the others came in 1973, 1970 and 1950.

test.q: Why could a private league require players to stand for the anthem?
choices: The First Amendment limits the government, not private employers
Congress passed a law requiring it
The Olympic Charter applies to all leagues
test.why: Leagues like the NBA and NFL are private employers that set workplace rules.

test.q: What did researchers find about television coverage of women's sports from 1989 to 2019?
choices: It rose to half of airtime
It stayed a small share, about five percent in 2019
test.why: The Cooky and Messner study found little change over thirty years.

write.prompt: Is a field, court or medal stand a workplace or a public square? Take a position. Support it with at least three dated cases from the unit, such as the 1965 AFL walkout, the 1968 podium, the 1996 NBA suspension, Rule 50 or the 2022 soccer agreements.
tips: Name each case with its date, place and the body that made the rule.
Tell the difference between a gesture during a ceremony and a refusal to play.
Show what each side argued before you judge it.
Use unit terms such as boycott, walkout, grievance and parallel institution.
End by saying which body you think should decide, and why.
